candidate.answerReason: If m machines are initially available, equal total work gives 3m=2(m+3). Thus m=6, and the job requires 18 machine-days.

methods.label: Count machine-days
methods.explanation:
Because all the machines work at the same rate, we can measure the job in machine-days, where one machine-day is the work of one machine in one day. The total number of machine-days must be the same in both plans.

Let \(m\) be the original number of machines. The two plans give
\[
3m=2(m+3)=2m+6,
\]
so \(m=6\). The whole job therefore requires
\[
3\cdot6=18
\]
machine-days. One machine supplies one machine-day of work each day, so it would take \(\boxed{18}\) days, choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
methods.levelReason: A simple work model leads to a linear equation with parentheses.

methods.label: Compare daily work rates
methods.explanation:
Treat the whole job as \(1\). The original group completes \(\frac13\) of the job per day, while the enlarged group completes \(\frac12\) per day. The difference is exactly the daily contribution of the three added machines:
\[
\frac12-\frac13=\frac16.
\]
Since these three machines work equally fast, one machine completes
\[
\frac16\div3=\frac1{18}
\]
of the job per day. Completing the whole job therefore takes \(\boxed{18}\) days, choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
methods.levelReason: This alternative uses only fractions and equal sharing of an added work rate.

candidate.annotationRationale: The shared target is modeling equal-rate work. The first method equates machine-day totals and solves a bracketed linear equation. The second subtracts daily job fractions and finds a unit rate. Their algebra and fraction procedures remain attached to their respective methods.
